title: Which learner, when?
objectives: Compare learners on one table of test scores, and choose one from the shape, size and noise of the data.
Explain why a learner chosen on the test rows cannot be reported on them.

screens.prose: Five learners, each after `StandardScaler`: logistic regression, 15-nearest neighbours, an RBF support vector machine, the 8-unit network and an additive logistic model. Each trains on 300 rows and is tested on 300 more. First problem: `make_street`, two overlapping clouds.
screens.question: Before the scores appear: how will the five compare?

options.text: All within a point of each other: when the truth is a line, nothing beats a line
The network well ahead, since it is the most flexible learner
options.why: You equated flexibility with skill. With a straight truth, flexibility has nothing to add.

options.text: Logistic regression well behind, since it can only draw a line
options.why: You forgot the truth here is a line. Logistic regression draws exactly the right shape.

options.text: Nearest neighbours well behind, since it has no model at all
options.why: You expected the model-free learner to lose. With 300 rows in 2 features it does fine.

hints.text: What shape is the best boundary for two overlapping round clouds?
A straight line between them.
Every learner can draw a line, so none can do better than one.

feedback.generic: Picture the best boundary, then ask who can draw it.

byKey.b: You expected the network to win by flexibility. It scored 0.9567, the lowest by a whisker.

explain.text: When the truth is a line, the linear model is already right and every flexible learner merely ties: 0.9633, 0.9633, 0.9633, 0.9567, 0.96. In a tie the simpler, more explainable learner wins by default. That is the edge case to remember.

screens.prose: Second problem: `make_rings`, class 1 in the centre and class 0 in a ring round it.
screens.question: Which learner fails?

options.text: Logistic regression
The additive model
options.why: You expected the additive model to fail. $f_1(x_1) + f_2(x_2)$ can make $x_1^2 + x_2^2$, a sum of one-feature curves.

options.text: Nearest neighbours
options.why: You expected the local learner to fail. A centre and a ring are exactly what neighbours see.

options.text: None of them
options.why: You missed that one learner can draw only straight lines.

hints.text: Which learner draws only straight boundaries?
The rings need a closed curve.
$x_1^2 + x_2^2$ is additive, so splines manage it; a line cannot.

feedback.correct: Logistic regression scores 0.5067; every flexible learner reaches about 0.98.
feedback.generic: Ask which learner cannot close a region.

explain.text: A curved boundary breaks the linear model, 0.5067, and any flexible learner mends it: 0.9767, 0.9767, 0.9733 and 0.98. The additive model wins here because $x_1^2 + x_2^2$ is a sum of one-feature curves. Two more seed pairs give the flexible learners 0.96 to 0.98.

screens.prose: Third problem: `make_quadrants`. Class 1 when the two features share a sign, with 10% of labels flipped at random.
screens.question: Which learners fail? Select all that apply.

options.text: Logistic regression
The additive model
Nearest neighbours
options.why: You expected the local learner to fail. Each quadrant is a solid block, which neighbours handle.

options.text: The support vector machine
options.why: You expected the kernel to fail. The RBF kernel can draw the four blocks.

hints.text: Is the rule a sum of a curve in $x_1$ and a curve in $x_2$?
Sharing a sign is about the product $x_1 x_2$.
Both the linear and the additive model cannot express a product.

feedback.correct: Logistic 0.4767 and additive 0.4567: both below a coin.
feedback.generic: Ask which learners can express a product of the features.

byKey.a: Right that logistic fails, but the additive model fails too: no sum of one-feature curves makes $x_1 x_2$.

explain.text: An interaction breaks both the linear and the additive model by construction: 0.4767 and 0.4567. The others reach 0.86, 0.8567 and 0.8467, and the 10% of flipped labels caps every learner near 0.90. **No learner is best on every problem.**

screens.prose: Fourth problem: `make_wide(60, 4)`, tested on `make_wide(300, 5)`. The signal sits in 2 columns, as in the street; the other 18 columns are noise, and there are only 60 training rows.
screens.question: Which learner suffers most?

options.text: Nearest neighbours: 18 noise columns swamp its distances
Logistic regression: 20 coefficients are too many for 60 rows
options.why: You expected the simplest to overfit first. Its 21 parameters do best here, 0.9233.

options.text: The network: it has the most parameters
options.why: You expected parameter count to decide. The network scored 0.9067, behind both linear-boundary learners.

options.text: None: with the signal in 2 columns all tie
options.why: You expected the noise columns to be ignored. Distances cannot ignore them.

hints.text: Which learner treats every column alike?
A distance adds 18 noisy squared gaps to 2 informative ones.
That is the curse of dimension for nearest neighbours.

feedback.correct: Nearest neighbours drops to 0.89; logistic regression leads at 0.9233.
feedback.generic: Think about what a distance between two rows is made of here.

explain.text: Few rows and many noisy features favour the simplest learner, 0.9233, and hurt the distance-based one most, 0.89. Neighbours in 20 dimensions are mostly neighbours in noise. The SVM scores 0.92, close behind.

screens.prose: Fifth problem: `make_noise`, labels up with chance 0.54 whatever the features say. On the 300 test rows the base rate of up is 0.55. Logistic regression and the SVM both score 0.5567.
screens.question: What is the $t$ statistic of a hit rate of 0.5567 against the base rate 0.55 on 300 rows? Give two decimal places.

hints.text: $t = (\hat h - b) / \sqrt{b(1 - b)/n}$.

feedback.correct: $t \approx 0.23$, far below 2: no edge at all.
feedback.generic: Use the base rate 0.55, not 0.5, in both places.

byKey.coin: That is the trap: you tested against a coin, 0.5. Against the base rate 0.55 the edge is 0.0067, $t \approx 0.23$.
byKey.nosqrt: You stopped at the gap, 0.0067. Divide it by the standard error $\sqrt{b(1 - b)/n} = 0.0287$.

explain.text: $0.0067 / 0.0287 \approx 0.23$: an edge of 2 rows in 300. On noise every learner sits at the base rate, and nearest neighbours, 0.4967, falls below it. Reading 0.5567 as skill is the trap.

screens.prose: The whole table. Each score is 1 minus a test error, and a test error splits as $E[\text{error}] = \text{bias}^2 + \text{variance} + \text{noise}$.
screens.question: What decides which learner to use?

options.text: The shape of the truth, the rows per feature, the noise, and what must be explained
The learner with the highest average score across the five rows
options.why: You averaged across problems. Your problem is one row, and the average hides that each learner fails somewhere.

options.text: The most flexible learner, since flexibility never hurts
options.why: You assumed flexibility is free. On the wide and noise rows it costs accuracy.

options.text: The newest learner, since it improves on the older ones
options.why: You ranked by age. The table has no winner across its rows.

hints.text: Look for a column that wins every row.
There is none: each learner loses somewhere.
Each row's winner follows from how its data were made.

feedback.correct: The data decide: shape, rows per feature, noise, and the need to explain.
feedback.generic: Find what made each row's winner win.

explain.text: Bias wins where the truth is simple or the rows are few; flexibility wins where the truth is curved and the rows are many. Noise caps everyone. Where scores tie, the learner you can explain wins.

screens.prose: What each learner needs before fitting. Logistic regression here carries scikit-learn's default ridge penalty. The additive model's spline columns are built per feature, each from its own range.
screens.question: Does each learner's score change if one feature is measured in different units? Type yes or no.

hints.text: Distances, gradient steps and penalties all read the units.
A penalty charges coefficients, and a coefficient's size depends on its feature's units.
Only the spline columns, each built from its own feature's range, are unaffected.

feedback.correct: Four yes, one no: scale before every learner that uses distances, gradients or a penalty.
feedback.generic: Ask whether each learner uses a distance, a gradient step or a penalty.

byKey.addyes: You expected the splines to need scaling. Each feature's basis is built from its own range, so its units drop out.

explain.text: Nearest neighbours and the SVM measure distances, the network takes gradient steps, and the penalised logistic model charges coefficients by size. Each changes with the units, so each sits after a scaler. The spline basis is rebuilt from each feature's own range, so its fit does not.

screens.prose: Fill the table in code. `PROBLEMS` maps a name to `(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test)` and `LEARNERS` maps a name to a function that builds a fresh pipeline, simplest first.
screens.question: Complete `fit_table(problems, learners)`, returning test accuracies rounded to 4 places.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def make_street(n, seed):            # two overlapping groups, a straight boundary is right
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    y = np.arange(n) % 2
    X = rng.normal(0, 0.8, (n, 2)) + np.where(y[:, None] == 1, 1.0, -1.0)
    return np.round(X, 3), y

def make_rings(n, seed):             # class 1 near the centre, class 0 in a ring round it
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    y = np.arange(n) % 2
    r = np.where(y == 1, rng.normal(0.8, 0.3, n), rng.normal(2.2, 0.4, n))
    a = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, n)
    return np.round(np.c_[r * np.cos(a), r * np.sin(a)], 3), y

def make_quadrants(n, seed):         # class 1 when the two features share a sign; 10% of labels flipped
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = rng.uniform(-2, 2, (n, 2))
    y = ((X[:, 0] * X[:, 1]) > 0).astype(int)
    flip = rng.random(n) < 0.1
    return np.round(X, 3), np.where(flip, 1 - y, y)

def make_wide(n, seed, p=20):        # make_street's signal in 2 columns, 18 columns of noise
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    y = np.arange(n) % 2
    X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, p))
    X[:, :2] = X[:, :2] * 0.8 + np.where(y[:, None] == 1, 1.0, -1.0)
    return np.round(X, 3), y

def make_noise(n, seed):             # labels are up with chance 0.54 whatever the features say
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 2))
    return np.round(X, 3), (rng.random(n) < 0.54).astype(int)

def make_stocks(seed):               # 60 shares: beta, and volatility in % a year; three groups of 20
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    rows, lab = [], []
    for g, (b, v) in enumerate([(0.6, 20.0), (1.4, 20.0), (1.0, 45.0)]):
        rows.append(np.c_[rng.normal(b, 0.12, 20), rng.normal(v, 5.0, 20)])
        lab += [g] * 20
    return np.round(np.vstack(rows), 2), np.array(lab)

def make_impact(n, seed):            # order size (% of daily volume) and price impact (bp): a square-root law
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    x = rng.uniform(0, 50, n)
    return np.round(x, 3), np.round(10 * np.sqrt(x) + rng.normal(0, 4, n), 3)

def make_additive(n, seed, interaction=0.0):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = rng.uniform(-2, 2, (n, 2))
    y = np.sin(1.5 * X[:, 0]) + 0.5 * X[:, 1] ** 2 + interaction * X[:, 0] * X[:, 1] + rng.normal(0, 0.3, n)
    return np.round(X, 3), np.round(y, 3)

from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, SplineTransformer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier

def _p(train, test):
    return train[0], train[1], test[0], test[1]

PROBLEMS = {
    "street": _p(make_street(300, 4), make_street(300, 5)),
    "rings": _p(make_rings(300, 7), make_rings(300, 8)),
    "quadrants": _p(make_quadrants(300, 3), make_quadrants(300, 4)),
    "wide": _p(make_wide(60, 4), make_wide(300, 5)),
    "noise": _p(make_noise(300, 4), make_noise(300, 5)),
}
LEARNERS = {   # simplest first
    "logistic": lambda: make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression()),
    "additive": lambda: make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SplineTransformer(n_knots=5), LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)),
    "knn": lambda: make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(15)),
    "svm": lambda: make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(C=1, gamma="scale")),
    "net": lambda: make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(8,), solver="lbfgs", alpha=0.01, random_state=0, max_iter=500)),
}

tests.call: fit_table({'street': PROBLEMS['street']}, {k: LEARNERS[k] for k in ('logistic', 'additive', 'knn', 'svm')})
fit_table({'quadrants': PROBLEMS['quadrants']}, {k: LEARNERS[k] for k in ('logistic', 'additive', 'knn', 'svm')})

widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests: single cells, two four-learner rows, a two-by-two block, and the network's rings cell. That cell is checked against a band from 0.95 to 0.99, because a network's score moves in the third place between runtimes. The first run loads scikit-learn.

hints.text: Two loops: problems outside, learners inside.
Build a fresh model with `make()` for every cell.
`round(m.score(X_test, y_test), 4)` fills the cell.

feedback.correct: The table reproduces: 0.5067 for logistic on the rings, 0.4567 for the additive model on the quadrants.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. The rings row for logistic should be 0.5067.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Each problem unpacks into four arrays.

explain.text: A fresh model per cell matters: reusing one fitted object would carry state between problems. The deterministic cells match to 4 places in any runtime. The network cell is tested only within a band.

screens.prose: Choosing a learner by its test score and then reporting that score is choosing on the test rows. Choose on a validation split instead: fit each learner on all but the last `n_val` training rows, score on those, refit the winner on all training rows, and report its test score once.

explain.text: On the street, logistic regression and nearest neighbours tie at 0.97, and the simpler one wins. On the noise, validation picks nearest neighbours at 0.51, and its honest test score is 0.4967, below the base rate. screens.prose: A researcher must predict next-day direction from 20 features on 750 days, split in time order. Up days run at about 54%.
screens.question: Which plan matches the table?

options.text: Logistic regression, then a network to compare; report the test hit rate beside the base rate
The RBF SVM first, since it never scored worst on any row of the table
options.why: You picked the safest column. The problem looks like the noise row, where the SVM's 0.5567 was the base rate.

options.text: Fit all five, keep the best on the test days, and report that score
options.why: That picks the winner on the test rows, so the reported score is biased upwards.

options.text: Nearest neighbours, since daily returns form local clusters
options.why: You trusted locality. With 20 noisy features, distances are mostly noise, as the wide row showed.

hints.text: Which rows look like this problem?
About 37 rows per feature and a weak signal: the wide row and the noise row.
Start simple, compare with one flexible learner, choose on validation, and report against the base rate.

feedback.correct: Start simple, compare once, choose on validation, report the hit rate with the base rate.
feedback.generic: Match the problem to a row first.

byKey.c: You chose on the test days. The best of five on the same rows overstates the edge.

explain.text: 750 days and 20 features is about 37 rows per feature with heavy noise: the wide and noise rows. Logistic regression is the first model and a network or SVM the comparison, chosen on a validation window. Report the test hit rate beside the base rate, and never pick the winner on the test rows.

ideas: No learner is best on every problem: a line wins ties when the truth is a line, curves need flexible learners, and interactions defeat additive models.
Few rows per feature and heavy noise favour the simplest learner; on pure noise every learner sits at the base rate.
Choose on a validation split, break ties towards the simpler model, and report the test score once, beside the base rate.
summary.trap: Picking the learner with the best test score and reporting that same score: the choice used the test rows.

quiz.prose: You re-run the rings row on two more pairs of seeds. The flexible learners score 0.98, 0.98, 0.9733 and 0.9833 on one pair, and 0.9633, 0.9667, 0.9567 and 0.9567 on the other.
quiz.question: What do the extra runs show?

options.text: The flexible learners' order changes with the sample; all sit in 0.96 to 0.98
The additive model is the best learner for rings, since it won the first pair
options.why: You trusted one seed pair. On the third pair it tied for last at 0.9567.

options.text: The network is unreliable, since it scored 0.9567
options.why: You singled out one cell. Every flexible learner moved by about 0.02.

options.text: Nothing: the first table already settled the order
options.why: You treated one split as the truth. Differences of a row or two flip between samples.

feedback.correct: Within about 0.02, the order is noise.
feedback.generic: Compare the spread across seeds with the gaps between learners.

explain.text: Across three seed pairs each flexible learner moves by about 0.02, more than the gaps between them. Concluding from one seed would crown a winner by luck. Only the logistic model's failure, near 0.5 every time, is real.

quiz.prose: Two learners tie on validation at 0.84: logistic regression with one interaction feature, and an RBF SVM.
quiz.question: Which do you choose, and why?

options.text: Logistic regression: on a tie the simpler, explainable model wins
The SVM, because a kernel captures more shapes in general
options.why: You chose capacity you do not need. On a tie, extra flexibility only adds variance.

options.text: Whichever has the higher test score
options.why: You broke the tie on the test rows, which makes them a second validation set.

options.text: Average their predictions, since two models beat one
options.why: You invented an ensemble. That may help, but it is a third model to validate, not a tie-break.

feedback.correct: A tie goes to the simpler model.
feedback.generic: Ask what the extra flexibility buys at equal validation accuracy.

explain.text: Equal validation accuracy means the extra flexibility bought nothing on these rows. The simpler model varies less on new data and can be explained to a risk committee. So the tie goes to logistic regression.

quiz.prose: A desk clusters 500 shares into groups with k-means and asks you to add it as a sixth column of the table.
quiz.question: What goes in its cells?

options.text: Nothing: clustering has no labels, so there is no test accuracy to report
Its inertia, since lower is better like an error
options.why: You treated inertia as a test error. It always falls with more groups and has no labels behind it.

options.text: The share of all shares that sit in the largest group
options.why: You invented a score. Group sizes say nothing about correctness.

options.text: Its purity, measured against the shares' true group labels
options.why: You assumed true labels exist. In unsupervised learning they do not.

feedback.correct: Unsupervised learning has no test accuracy.
feedback.generic: What would a test accuracy compare against?

explain.text: A test accuracy compares predictions with labels, and clustering has none. Purity worked earlier only because we planted the groups. That is the edge case where the table cannot be filled at all.
